The Holter tracings show ST‑segment elevation in I, aVL and V1–V5 immediately before the polymorphic VT, consistent with acute/transient transmural ischemia in the anterolateral/anteroseptal distribution. Coronary angiography and IVUS demonstrate significant atherosclerotic disease (diffuse 50–90% LAD stenosis with plaque burden 74% and MLA 5.92 mm2; 80% mid‑RCA lesion). The combination of (1) documented polymorphic VT, (2) transient ST‑elevation just before the arrhythmia, (3) angiographic/IVUS evidence of high plaque burden in LAD, and (4) cardiovascular risk factor (diabetes) makes ischemia‑induced ventricular arrhythmia from coronary artery disease the most likely cause. Normal troponin and a normal ECG at admission do not exclude brief ischemia or transient plaque rupture/spasm that provoked the arrhythmia. Long‑QT/torsades is unlikely given normal QTc. Primary channelopathies (Brugada, early repolarization/idiopathic VF) or structural cardiomyopathies (ARVC) are possible but less likely given the clear coronary atherosclerosis and the ST changes preceding the VT that localize to ischemia-susceptible territories.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Ischemia‑induced ventricular arrhythmia (acute/transient myocardial ischemia/acute coronary syndrome causing polymorphic VT) secondary to significant coronary atherosclerotic disease (LAD ± RCA lesions)
2. Coronary vasospasm (vasospastic angina) causing transient ST‑elevation and polymorphic VT
3. Brugada syndrome (acute Brugada ECG pattern precipitating polymorphic VT) — less likely given distribution of ST changes and presence of CAD
4. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation / early repolarization–associated VF (primary electrical disorder causing polymorphic VT) — less likely given CAD and ischemic ECG changes
5. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) or other structural cardiomyopathy with ventricular arrhythmia — less likely due to normal echocardiogram and localization of ischemic ECG changes
